metadata.name: webServerCryptoChecker default policy
metadata.description: The editable policy: how each TLS version, cipher suite, key-exchange group and signature algorithm is classified, and how those classifications become a score and a grade. Change the criterion by editing this file, not the code.

protocols.note: POODLE; SSL 3.0 must not be used.
DROWN; SSL 2.0 is broken and must not be used.

_comment_security_strength: Effective security strength in bits (NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5): the weakest link across the classes the server would use. 'symmetric' and 'hash' are keyword->bits pairs scanned in order (most specific first) against the cipher-suite and signature-scheme names; 'asymmetric' maps the certificate key -- RSA/DH modulus via ascending thresholds, an EC field size divided by 'ec_divisor', or a named curve -- to bits; 'levels' bucket the effective bits (ascending, the highest match wins). Re-tuning the numbers here re-tunes the report without touching code.
_comment_vulnerabilities: Known vulnerabilities detectable from what a server offers on the wire. Adding one is editing this list, not the code: 'detection' is a tree of conditions the tool evaluates -- protocol (a version is supported), cipher_tag (an offered suite carries a shape-tag), combined with all/any/not. The static-RSA surface behind ROBOT is flagged passively here (a suite without forward secrecy); confirming a live Bleichenbacher oracle is the separate active probe in tls/robot.py (behind --active), like Heartbleed. SSL 2.0 is probed on its own (it is not a TLS record) and surfaced as the 'ssl2' protocol, so DROWN is detected here like any other protocol condition.

vulnerabilities.name: DROWN
vulnerabilities.description: The server speaks SSL 2.0, which is broken in itself and lets an attacker decrypt modern TLS_RSA sessions that share its RSA key (the DROWN cross-protocol attack).
vulnerabilities.remediation: Disable SSL 2.0 everywhere the certificate's RSA key is used.

vulnerabilities.name: POODLE
vulnerabilities.description: SSL 3.0 is vulnerable to the POODLE padding-oracle attack.

vulnerabilities.name: Sweet32 (64-bit block cipher)
vulnerabilities.description: 3DES has a 64-bit block, so a long-lived connection leaks plaintext via a birthday collision.

vulnerabilities.name: RC4 keystream biases
vulnerabilities.description: RC4's keystream is biased, which allows recovery of repeated plaintext.

vulnerabilities.name: Export-grade key exchange (FREAK / Logjam)
vulnerabilities.description: Export-grade cipher suites use deliberately small keys and enable downgrade attacks.

vulnerabilities.name: Cleartext (NULL) cipher
vulnerabilities.description: A NULL cipher provides no encryption at all.

vulnerabilities.name: Anonymous key exchange
vulnerabilities.description: Anonymous cipher suites provide no authentication and permit an undetected man-in-the-middle.

vulnerabilities.name: Single DES
vulnerabilities.description: Single DES has a 56-bit key and is brute-forceable.

vulnerabilities.name: BEAST
vulnerabilities.description: CBC suites under TLS 1.0/1.1 are exposed to BEAST, though most clients now mitigate it.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Prefer TLS 1.2 or higher and AEAD cipher suites.

vulnerabilities.name: Key exchange without forward secrecy
vulnerabilities.description: A suite negotiates the session key with static RSA (or static DH), so recording the traffic today and stealing the server key later decrypts it. Static-RSA key exchange is also the Bleichenbacher/ROBOT padding-oracle surface; confirming a live oracle needs an active probe.
vulnerabilities.remediation: Offer only ECDHE (or DHE) suites; disable static RSA and static DH key exchange.
